name: Zane Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'm not much of a talker, so you might have to pull it out of me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the family payments processing centre on the business park outside town, big grey building, about four hundred of us. I don't do phones, I do the back office: new births, a child leaving school, a parent moving in or out, and I update the claim and work out the new payment. I've got my own way of working through the queue, oldest first, with a paper checklist I made in my first year. I like that it's quiet and that you finish things. I don't like the new system updates, every few months they move the buttons and it takes me a week to get my speed back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd guess happens, to be honest. Most new things at work turn out smaller than the posters say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise about not much. At darts on Thursday I'd probably say the computers still can't spell my surname, which is true. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. My job's steady, the centre's been there twenty years, and my rent is cheap because the flat's small. Nothing in my life really needs to change, and I'd like it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the queue the way I do it. Keep the hundred a month going into savings by standing order, like I have since I started. If they brought in some small tool for routine bits, I'd use it if I had to, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use a tool if you had to. What if it was optional?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't. I'm quick with my checklist and I know where I am with it. If it saves my colleagues ten minutes, good for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. My mum's on her own since my dad died and I do her shopping on Saturdays, so I'd never want to move far. But the centre isn't going anywhere, so that's fine.

say: I'd say it was **a lot of noise** about not much.
At **darts** I'd joke that the computers still can't spell my surname.
think: My job is **steady** and the centre has been there **twenty years**.
With **cheap rent** and simple needs, nothing in my life needs to change.
do: Keep working the queue **oldest first** with my paper checklist.
Keep the **hundred a month** standing order into savings.
S0.quote: Most new things at work turn out smaller than the posters say.
fieldNote: He likes **routine** and finds real comfort in a quiet, finished queue.
He'd skip optional tools, trusting his **own checklist** over anything new.
His mother living nearby **ties him** to the area, which matters later.

steps.text: Keep working the claims queue oldest first with his checklist
Keep the hundred-a-month standing order into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one's less comfortable. Updating claims is the kind of checking it talks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see what it actually does before anyone panics. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything. I'd say that to my team leader too, though I'd be less sure inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is one of the first to go. What I do is take a form, check it against the rules, and change a number. If a computer can read the form, there's not much of me left. I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do anything big straight away, I'd wait and see who they move first. But I'd stop buying the takeaway twice a week and push the savings up to two hundred. And I'd start keeping an eye on the jobs board at the council, because they still need people in person for some things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, and then a sort of tight feeling that sticks around. I'd probably not say anything about it to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they stopped replacing people on my floor, or if Ray, my team leader, got moved. He's been there fifteen years. If they can move him, they can move anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new tools if it might keep you in the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn what they made me learn. I know that's probably not enough. I'm just not someone who picks this stuff up fast, and I'd rather be honest about it.

say: I'd say **let's see** what it does before anyone panics.
I'd remind people that **every few years** a new thing is meant to change everything.
think: My job is take a form, **check the rules**, change a number, so it goes early.
If a computer reads the form, there's **not much of me** left in the work.
do: **Wait and see** who gets moved first before doing anything big.
Drop the **twice-weekly takeaway** and raise savings to two hundred a month.
Watch the **council jobs board** for in-person roles.
feel: **Uneasy**, settling into a tight feeling he wouldn't share with anyone.
S1.quote: What I do is take a form, check it against the rules, and change a number. If a computer can read the form, there's not much of me left.
fieldNote: His public line is **wait and see**, but privately he sees his job as exposed.
He'd learn only **what's required**, and admits that probably isn't enough.
His trigger to act is his team leader **being moved**.

steps.text: Wait to see who on his floor gets moved first
Raise the savings standing order to two hundred a month
Check the council jobs board weekly for in-person roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not long at all. I've had the same mobile phone longer than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should slow it down. I'm not a politics person, but I'd sign the petitions. I'd say the government should have a plan for the four hundred of us in that building, because there's nothing else like it near here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out of work by 2029. All of my job is thinking at a desk, none of it is hands-on, so the robots coming later doesn't buy me anything. I've got about three months saved, and I don't know what I'd be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything except rent, food and the bike. Ask my mum if I could move back into her spare room, which would also mean I'm there for her. And look at hands-on jobs where you can start without a degree, maybe the electrician apprenticeship the college runs, because robots doing that are a few more years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake. I don't really have a plan B, and that's the worst bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it feel to move back in with your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassing, at twenty-seven. But she'd be glad of the company and I'd be glad of the rent. We'd get on fine, as long as she doesn't rearrange my things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is an apprenticeship realistic for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm good with my hands, I fix my own bike. The money is low for the first two years. But it's that or nothing, so I'd make it realistic.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and someone should slow it down.
I'd **sign petitions** and ask for a plan for the **four hundred** staff at the centre.
think: My job is all **desk thinking**, so the robot delay buys me nothing.
With **three months saved**, I don't know what I'd be good at.
do: Cut spending to **rent, food** and the bike.
Ask my mum about moving into her **spare room**.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake with no plan B.
S2.quote: I've got about three months saved, and I don't know what I'd be good at.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that **none of his job** is hands-on, so AGI hits him on day one.
Moving back to his mum is both **a cost saving** and a way to care for her.
His bike repairs give him a **concrete reason** to try an apprenticeship.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and bike costs
Move into his mum's spare room to save rent
Apply for the college's electrician apprenticeship
Sign petitions for a plan for the processing centre's staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Still not much when you're slow to change, like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: let's see. But I'd add that five years is enough for the government and the centre to plan for us, and if they don't, that's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is dangerous for someone like me. I'd tell myself there's loads of time, and then in 2030 I'd still be doing the queue with my checklist. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening electrical course at the college in the second year, once I've seen whether it's really happening. I'd keep saving two hundred a month so I've got more like eight months by 2030. And I'd ask Ray to tell me straight if he hears anything about the centre's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in the background, all the time. Not panicking, just never quite switched off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until the second year. Why not start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to be sure. If I spend money on a course and nothing happens, I've wasted it. I know that's exactly how people get caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working as an electrician, probably for someone else, living somewhere small near my mum. Not exciting. But steady, which is all I've ever wanted.

say: I'd add that five years is enough for the government to **plan for us**.
think: Five years is **dangerous** because I'd tell myself there's loads of time.
I could still be on the **same queue** in 2030, and I know it.
do: Start an **evening electrical course** in the second year once it looks real.
Save **two hundred a month** to reach about eight months by 2030.
Ask my team leader to tell me **straight** about the centre's future.
feel: **Worried in the background**, never quite switched off.
S3.quote: Five years is dangerous for someone like me. I'd tell myself there's loads of time, and then in 2030 I'd still be doing the queue with my checklist.
fieldNote: He sees his own **delay habit** as the biggest risk, and still chooses to wait a year.
He names the contradiction himself: waiting is how people get **caught out**.
His goal is just to be **steady again** as an electrician near his mum.

steps.text: Wait a year to confirm the change before spending on courses
Start an evening electrical course at the college in year two
Save two hundred a month to reach eight months' cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. I'd be thirty-seven. My mum would be well into her seventies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at darts it's ages away and to stop worrying. I'd probably believe it, at least for the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough to change trades properly, and I'd have no excuse. The centre would probably shrink slowly before 2036 anyway, so I'd see people leaving and that would push me. The question is whether I go before I'm pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for two or three years and keep saving. Around 2029 I'd start the electrician course in the evenings and qualify by about 2032. I'd stay near my mum the whole way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with a worry I'd keep putting in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see people leaving. Who would push you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ray left, that would do it. Or if the canteen closed, honestly. The canteen is the heart of the building. If they shut the canteen, it means they've stopped planning for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first. Maybe the summer week away with my mates, so I've got the course fees covered when I start. I'd rather pay for it myself than wait for some scheme.

say: I'd tell the **darts** crowd it's ages away and to stop worrying.
I'd probably **believe it** myself for the first few years.
think: Ten years is enough to **change trades** properly, so I'd have no excuse.
The real question is whether I go **before I'm pushed**.
do: Carry on as normal for **two or three years**, saving steadily.
Start the **electrician course** around 2029 and qualify by about 2032.
Skip the **summer week away** to cover course fees.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with a worry he keeps putting in a drawer.
S4.quote: The canteen is the heart of the building. If they shut the canteen, it means they've stopped planning for people.
fieldNote: He'd wait **two or three years**, which fits his resistant style even with plenty of warning.
His signal to move is **small and physical**: a team leader leaving or the canteen closing.
He prefers to **fund retraining himself** rather than rely on a scheme.

steps.text: Carry on in the processing job for two or three years
Skip the summer week away to cover course fees

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nothing lined up and about three months of savings. What would help is someone paying for the apprenticeship wage gap, so you could retrain without losing your flat, and a real plan for big offices like ours before it happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about my mum. Everybody talks about jobs, but if I lose my job I'm also the one doing my mum's shopping and her hospital trips. Whatever I do next has to be close to her.

headlineQuote: If I lose my job I'm also the one doing my mum's shopping and her hospital trips. Whatever I do next has to be close to her.
portrait: Zane is a 27-year-old **back-office processor** of family payments at a large regional centre.
He works from a **paper checklist**, never uses AI, and loves a quiet, finished queue.
He says **let's see** in public but privately knows his form-checking job is exposed.
In the AGI pictures he'd move toward an **electrician apprenticeship**, though he admits he'd delay.
Caring for his **widowed mum** nearby shapes every plan he makes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with nothing lined up and about three months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Help covering the **apprenticeship wage gap** while retraining.
A **real plan** for big processing offices before the change.
